chapters.name: Chapter 1: Starting a project the right way

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What makes work a project
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify whether a piece of work is a project and name its phases and constraints.
This lesson builds toward: Given a description of a piece of work, you will identify whether it is a project and name its life-cycle phases and main constraints, correctly for at least 4 of 5 examples.
A project is temporary work to create something new: it has a start, an end and a unique result. Opening a food truck, moving an office, running a voter drive or building a website are projects. Cooking the same lunch menu every day, or answering the phones each shift, is ongoing operations, not a project.
Most projects move through phases. A simple way to see them: start (agree why and what), plan (how, when, who, how much), do the work, watch and control it, and close (hand it over and record lessons learned). PMI calls the people and practices that guide this "project management".
Every project is limited by constraints. The classic three are scope (what you will deliver), schedule (time) and cost (money). Quality, resources and risk matter too. If one changes, the others feel it: add scope with the same deadline and you need more people or money, or quality drops.
Step by step:
- Ask: does this work have a clear start and end?
- Ask: does it create something new or different?
- If yes to both, it is a project. If it repeats every day, it is operations.
- Name the phase it is in now and its tightest constraint.
Words to know:
- Project: temporary work with a start, an end and a unique result.
- Operations: ongoing, repeated work that keeps a business running.
- Constraint: a limit on the project, such as time, money or scope.
- Scope: all the work and results the project will deliver, and nothing more.
- Life cycle: the phases a project moves through from start to close.
Official sources:
- Project Management Institute: What is project management?
Try it now: Write down five pieces of work from your life, your job or your military service. Mark each one P (project) or O (operations). For each project, write its tightest constraint: scope, time or money.
You can now tell a project from ongoing operations, name its phases and say which constraint is tightest.

check.q: Which of these is a project?
options: Opening a second store location by June
check.why: Opening a new location is temporary, has an end date and creates something new.

check.q: The sponsor adds three new features but keeps the same deadline and budget. What is most likely to suffer?
options: Nothing; scope does not affect other constraints
Quality, unless more time, people or money are added
check.why: Scope, schedule and cost are linked; more scope with the same time and money puts pressure on quality.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The project charter and your stakeholders
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page charter and a stakeholder list for a small project.
This lesson builds toward: For a small real project, you will write a one-page project charter and a stakeholder list with each person's interest and influence, including goal, scope in and out, sponsor, deadline and a measurable success measure.
The project charter is the document that officially starts a project. It names the sponsor (the person who approves and funds it) and gives the project manager authority to use people and money. Think of it as the mission order: no charter, no project.
A good one-page charter has: the purpose (why), a goal with a measure ("open the food pantry's online sign-up by 1 March, with 50 families signed up in the first month"), scope in and scope out, the deadline and major milestones, the budget, the main risks, and the sponsor's name.
Stakeholders are everyone who affects the project or is affected by it: the sponsor, the team, customers, neighbors, inspectors, suppliers. List them, then place each on a simple grid of influence (high or low) and interest (high or low). High influence and high interest: manage them closely. High influence, low interest: keep them satisfied. Low influence, high interest: keep them informed. Low and low: check in now and then.
Step by step:
- Write the purpose in one sentence.
- Write the goal with a number and a date.
- List what is in scope and what is out.
- Add deadline, milestones, budget and sponsor.
- List stakeholders and place each on the influence and interest grid.
Words to know:
- Project charter: the document that officially starts the project and gives the project manager authority.
- Sponsor: the person or group that approves, funds and supports the project.
- Stakeholder: anyone who affects the project or is affected by it.
- Milestone: an important point in the schedule, with no length of its own, such as "permit approved".
Try it now: Pick a small real project, such as a family reunion, a church fundraiser, a yard sale or cleaning up a storage room at work. Write a one-page charter with every part above, then list at least five stakeholders and place each on the grid.
You can now write a one-page charter and decide how to work with each stakeholder.

check.q: Which goal is best for a charter?
options: "Open online sign-up by 1 March with 50 families signed up in the first month"
check.why: A good goal has a number and a date, so everyone can tell whether it was met.

check.q: The city inspector has high influence but little interest in your project. How do you treat the inspector?
options: Keep them satisfied: meet their needs without heavy updates
check.why: High influence, low interest stakeholders are kept satisfied so they do not block the project.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Breaking down the work and finding the critical path
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a work breakdown structure and a schedule, and mark the critical path.
This lesson builds toward: Given a project goal and a list of tasks with durations, you will build a work breakdown structure and a schedule that marks the critical path, with every dependency shown and the critical path length calculated correctly.
A work breakdown structure (WBS) splits the whole project into smaller pieces of deliverables, level by level, until each piece is small enough to estimate and give to one person. The smallest piece is a work package. If it is not in the WBS, it is not in the project.
Next, list the tasks, how long each takes (duration) and which must finish before another can start (dependencies). Draw them as boxes with arrows, left to right. Example: A, get the permit (2 days); B, build the booth (3 days, after A); C, order signs (1 day, after A); D, set up at the fair (2 days, after B and C).
Add up each path from start to end. A-B-D takes 2 + 3 + 2 = 7 days. A-C-D takes 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 days. The longest path is the critical path: it sets the shortest possible finish, 7 days. A delay on A, B or D delays the whole project. C has float (slack) of 7 - 5 = 2 days: it can slip 2 days without moving the finish.
Step by step:
- Write the project's main deliverables as the first level of the WBS.
- Break each one down until a piece is small enough for one person to estimate.
- List tasks with durations and what each one must wait for.
- Draw boxes and arrows, then add up every path.
- The longest path is the critical path; the others have float.
Words to know:
- Work breakdown structure (WBS): a tree that splits the project's deliverables into smaller pieces.
- Work package: the smallest piece in the WBS, small enough to estimate and assign.
- Dependency: a link that means one task must finish (or start) before another can.
- Critical path: the longest chain of linked tasks; it sets the earliest the project can finish.
- Float (slack): how long a task can slip without delaying the project's finish.
- Gantt chart: a bar chart that shows each task on a calendar.
Try it now: Take the project from your charter. Draw a WBS with at least two levels on paper. Then list five to eight tasks with durations and dependencies, draw them as boxes and arrows, add up each path, and circle the critical path. Write the float of one task that is not on it.
You can now break a project into a WBS, build a simple schedule and find the critical path and float.

check.q: Path 1 takes 9 days and Path 2 takes 6 days. What is the critical path, and how long is the project?
check.why: The longest path is the critical path, and it sets the shortest finish: 9 days.

check.q: A task has 2 days of float and slips 1 day. What happens to the finish date?
check.why: A task can slip up to its float without delaying the finish.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Risks, issues and change control
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Record risks in a risk register and send a change request through change control.
This lesson builds toward: For the same project, you will record risks in a risk register and handle a change request through change control, with a score, a response and one owner for every risk, and no change made without approval.
A risk is something that MIGHT happen and would affect the project. An issue is a problem that is happening NOW. Write risks down early in a risk register: the risk, its probability (how likely, 1 to 5), its impact (how bad, 1 to 5), a score (probability times impact), a response and one owner.
There are four main responses to a threat. Avoid it (change the plan so it cannot happen). Transfer it (move it to someone else, for example with insurance or a contract). Mitigate it (make it less likely or less harmful). Accept it (do nothing now, but watch it, and maybe keep some time or money in reserve). Example: rain at an outdoor event, probability 3, impact 4, score 12; response: mitigate by renting a tent; owner: Maria.
Changes will come. Scope creep is when work is added without approval. To stop it, use change control: write a change request, check its effect on scope, time, cost, quality and risk, have the right person (often the sponsor or a change board) approve or reject it, then update the plan and the change log. No approval, no change.
Step by step:
- List what could go wrong (and what could go better than planned).
- Score each risk: probability x impact.
- Choose a response: avoid, transfer, mitigate or accept.
- Give each risk one owner.
- For any change: write it down, check the impact, get approval, then update the plan.
Words to know:
- Risk: something uncertain that might happen and would affect the project.
- Issue: a problem that is already happening.
- Risk register: a table of risks with scores, responses and owners.
- Mitigate: make a risk less likely or less harmful.
- Scope creep: work added to the project without approval.
- Change control: the process to review, approve or reject changes before they are made.
Try it now: Make a risk register for your project in a spreadsheet or on paper with columns: risk, probability, impact, score, response, owner. Add at least three risks. Then write one change request someone might ask for, and note its effect on time and cost and who must approve it.
You can now keep a risk register and stop scope creep with change control.

check.q: A risk has probability 4 and impact 3. What is its score?
A team member adds a new feature because a customer asked in the hallway. What went wrong?
options: The risk register was too long
Scope creep: the change skipped change control
check.why: Changes must be written, checked for impact and approved before work starts.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Predictive, Agile or hybrid: choosing the approach
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a predictive, Agile or hybrid approach for a project and give the reasons.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short project scenario, you will choose a predictive, Agile or hybrid approach and explain the choice, giving at least two reasons from the scenario.
A predictive approach (sometimes called waterfall or plan-based) plans the scope, schedule and cost up front and follows the plan, with changes going through change control. It fits work where the requirements are clear and stable and changes are costly, such as building a ramp, moving a warehouse or a construction job with permits.
An Agile approach delivers in short cycles (iterations or sprints), gets feedback each time and adjusts the plan. It fits work where needs are unclear or will change, such as a new app or a new service where you must learn what customers want. Scrum and Kanban are common Agile methods.
A hybrid approach mixes them: for example, a predictive plan for buying equipment and a fixed opening date, with Agile sprints for the website and marketing. Whatever the approach, someone must understand the requirements: what the customer truly needs. Gathering, writing and checking requirements is called business analysis, and it is part of what the CAPM covers.
Step by step:
- Ask: are the requirements clear and stable?
- Ask: how costly is a change late in the project?
- Ask: can we deliver and get feedback in small pieces?
- Clear and costly to change: predictive. Unclear and easy to deliver in pieces: Agile. A mix: hybrid.
Words to know:
- Predictive approach: plan scope, time and cost up front, then follow the plan; also called waterfall.
- Agile approach: deliver in short cycles, get feedback and adjust the plan.
- Hybrid approach: a mix of predictive and Agile parts in one project.
- Requirement: a need the result must meet, such as "customers can pay by phone".
- Business analysis: finding, writing and checking what the customer truly needs.
Official sources:
- Manifesto for Agile Software Development
- The Scrum Guide
Try it now: Read these three: (1) paving a church parking lot with a fixed permit and budget; (2) a new delivery app where customers keep asking for changes; (3) opening a restaurant with a fixed date and a new online ordering site. Write predictive, Agile or hybrid for each, with two reasons. Then decide which approach fits your own project and why.
You can now choose a predictive, Agile or hybrid approach and explain why it fits.

check.q: A team is building a new app and does not yet know which features customers will use. Which approach fits best?
options: Predictive, with every feature fixed now
Agile, delivering small pieces and getting feedback
Wait until customers send a full list
check.why: Unclear needs fit Agile: short cycles and feedback show what customers want.

check.q: Paving a parking lot with a fixed permit, a fixed budget and clear specifications fits which approach?
check.why: Clear, stable requirements and costly late changes fit a predictive plan.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: The CAPM: checking the rules and planning your test
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a dated CAPM study and test plan from PMI's official pages.
This lesson builds toward: Using PMI's official pages, you will build a dated CAPM study and test plan, with eligibility checked, the exam content outline listed and a target test date.
The Certified Associate in Project Management (CAPM) is an entry-level credential granted only by the Project Management Institute (PMI). It is meant for people starting out, so it does not ask for years of project experience the way PMI's Project Management Professional (PMP) does. PMI does require some project management education before you take the exam. This course prepares you; it is not the credential, and it may or may not count toward PMI's education hours, so check pmi.org.
Before you plan, read PMI's official CAPM page and the CAPM handbook and Exam Content Outline it links to. Write down: who is eligible, how many hours of education you need and what counts, the current fee (PMI members and non-members may pay different amounts), how and where you can take the exam, and how to keep the credential (it must be renewed). Recent outlines have covered project management basics, predictive methods, Agile methods and business analysis, but use the outline PMI shows today.
Veterans: the GI Bill may pay back licensing and certification test fees. Check VA's test-fee page and its GI Bill Comparison Tool to see whether a test is approved. Outside the US, PMI has local chapters in many countries; look one up on pmi.org for study groups. Beware of anyone selling "guaranteed pass" or real exam questions: that breaks PMI's rules and can cost you the credential.
Step by step:
- Open pmi.org and find the CAPM page, the handbook and the Exam Content Outline.
- Write down eligibility, education hours, fee, exam format and renewal rules.
- Pick a target test date 8 to 12 weeks away (or what fits your life).
- Break your study into a WBS by exam topic, with milestones and practice tests.
- Add a risk register: work hours, family, test anxiety, cost.
Words to know:
- CAPM: Certified Associate in Project Management, an entry-level credential from PMI.
- PMI: Project Management Institute, the organization that grants the CAPM and PMP.
- Exam Content Outline: PMI's official list of the topics an exam covers.
- PMP: Project Management Professional, PMI's credential for experienced project managers.
- Eligibility: the requirements you must meet before you can apply for the exam.
Official sources:
- PMI: Certified Associate in Project Management (CAPM)
- PMI: Certifications
- U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs: Reimbursement for licensing or certification test fees
Try it now: Final task: open PMI's CAPM page and write down eligibility, education hours, fee and the exam topics. Then plan your CAPM preparation as a project: a one-page charter with a target test date, a WBS of your study by topic, a dated schedule with milestones and the critical path marked, and a risk register with at least three risks. Add the list of PMI pages you checked.
You can now check PMI's current CAPM rules and build your own dated study and test plan.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Charter The goal is vague or has no date, or scope in and out is missing. One page with purpose, a goal with a number and a date, scope in and out, sponsor and milestones. Also lists stakeholders with influence and interest and how each will be kept informed. WBS and schedule Tasks are listed with no breakdown, durations or dependencies. A WBS with at least two levels and a dated schedule with milestones, dependencies and the critical path marked. Shows the float on non-critical tasks and the critical path length is calculated correctly. Risk register Fewer than three risks, or risks with no response or owner. At least three risks, each with probability, impact, score, a response and one owner. Uses more than one type of response and includes a change-control note for how the plan will be changed. Approach No approach chosen, or no reason given. Names predictive, Agile or hybrid for the study plan and gives two reasons. Shows how the approach is used, for example weekly study cycles with a review. Official CAPM rules checked Fees, hours or exam topics copied from an unofficial source or left out. Lists eligibility, education hours, fee and exam topics from PMI's pages, with the page names. Also lists help with costs (for example GI Bill or employer support) and a local PMI chapter or study group. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and resubmit.

check.why: Only PMI grants the CAPM; courses only prepare you.

check.q: Where should you check the current CAPM fee and education hours?
options: PMI's official CAPM page and handbook on pmi.org
check.why: Fees and requirements change; PMI's own pages are the official source.
